actions.label: kubectl rollout restart deploy/links-api
actions.say: Fresh pods start, run for about six minutes, and get OOMKilled again. Restarting resets the clock; it fixes nothing.

actions.label: Scale to 6 replicas
actions.say: Six pods now, all creeping up towards 2 GiB. The new ones start dying ten minutes later. More copies of a pod that does not fit is more OOMKills.

actions.label: Raise -Xmx to 3g
actions.say: The heap can now grow past the 2 GiB limit on its own. Pods die faster: the kernel kills them as soon as the heap fills.

actions.label: Raise the memory limit to 3Gi (request too)
actions.say: Pods stop dying and the error rate drops to zero. You bought headroom, but -Xmx2g still assumes the whole limit is heap.

actions.label: Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 (drop -Xmx) and roll out
actions.say: The rollout finishes: heap capped at 1.5 GiB, about 300 MiB left for metaspace, threads and buffers. Memory settles at 1.8 GiB and the restarts stop.

actions.label: kubectl rollout undo (back to 4.11.3)
actions.say: Back on 4.11.3: smaller click batches, so less is allocated at once. It holds for now, but 4.11.3 still has -Xmx2g in a 2 GiB pod.

choices: A memory leak in the analytics batch, which eventually throws OutOfMemoryError
The JVM process outgrows its 2 GiB cgroup limit: the heap alone may use all 2 GiB, and metaspace, threads and buffers come on top, so the kernel SIGKILLs it
The liveness probe times out during long GC pauses, so the kubelet restarts the container
The node is out of memory and the kubelet evicts the pod
diagnosis.explain: Exit 137 is 128 + 9, a SIGKILL. There is no Java OutOfMemoryError because the heap never ran out: the kernel killed the whole process when the cgroup hit 2 GiB. The pod events say OOMKilled, not a probe failure or an eviction.

choices: Restart the pods every few hours with a CronJob
Remove the memory limit so the pod can use what it needs
Size the heap as a share of the limit (MaxRAMPercentage around 75%) and alert on container memory against its limit
Raise -Xmx until the GC pauses go away
fix.explain: The heap must leave room for everything else the JVM uses. A percentage keeps that true when someone changes the limit later. Removing the limit just moves the OOM to the node.

hints: What does exit code 137 mean, in numbers?
Compare what the JVM is allowed to use with what the container is allowed to use.
levels.truth: links-api runs Java with -Xms2g -Xmx2g in a pod with a 2Gi memory limit. Heap plus metaspace (~150MB), 210 thread stacks (~210MB), code cache and GC (~160MB) and direct buffers exceed 2Gi under load, so the kernel OOM-kills the process (exit 137, reason OOMKilled). No Java OOM error is ever logged. Revision 11 raised the heap to 2g; revision 12 made analytics batches bigger, which pushed memory over sooner. The node itself has plenty of free memory. Liveness probes are fine.
levels.debrief: The JVM was told it could use all 2 GiB for heap inside a 2 GiB container, so everything else it needs pushed it over the cgroup limit and the kernel killed it. Exit 137 with no Java error is the tell.

actions.label: Restart the API pods
actions.say: New pods connect, send their first query, and join the same lock queue. Nothing changes.

actions.label: Scale the API to 20 pods
actions.say: More pods, more connections, all waiting on the same lock. pgbouncer's queue doubles.

actions.label: SELECT pg_cancel_backend(48990)  (the ALTER)
actions.say: The ALTER is cancelled. Its place in the lock queue frees up and 400 queued queries run in a second. Latency is back to normal.

actions.label: SELECT pg_terminate_backend(48211)  (the 41-minute report)
actions.say: The report dies, the ALTER gets its lock, finishes in 40 ms, and the queue drains. Site back. The analytics team will ask where their export went.

actions.label: Restart Postgres
actions.say: Postgres restarts: 90 seconds of total outage, every connection dropped, then everything comes back. It worked, the hard way.

actions.label: VACUUM ANALYZE links
actions.say: The VACUUM itself waits in the lock queue behind the ALTER. Nothing moves.

diagnosis.prompt: Why did adding a column take everything down?
choices: The ALTER waits for an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock behind a 41-minute report query, and every query on links queues behind the waiting ALTER until the pool is exhausted
Adding a NOT NULL column with a default rewrites the whole table, which pins the CPU
The report query is so heavy that it starves the database of I/O
pgbouncer crashed and stopped handing out connections
diagnosis.explain: The database CPU is idle; everything is waiting on a lock. pg_blocking_pids shows the chain: report → ALTER → everyone. Lock requests queue in order, so a waiting ACCESS EXCLUSIVE blocks even plain SELECTs that would not conflict with the report.

choices: Never run migrations during the day
Give pgbouncer a much bigger pool
Run every migration inside a long transaction so it can be rolled back
Set a short lock_timeout on migrations and retry them, and keep long analytics queries off the primary (a replica, with statement_timeout)
fix.explain: With lock_timeout = 2s the ALTER gives up instead of queueing everyone behind it, and a retry loop gets it in when the table is quiet. Long reports belong on a replica.

hints: The database is idle. What is everything waiting for?
levels.truth: pid 48211 is a 41-minute analytics report (SELECT on links JOIN clicks) holding AccessShareLock on links. Migration 0142 (pid 48990) runs ALTER TABLE links ADD COLUMN archived boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false, which needs AccessExclusiveLock and is queued behind the report. Every later query on links (reads and writes) queues behind the ALTER. pgbouncer has 100 server connections all stuck and 412 clients waiting. Database CPU is idle (92% idle); memory and disk are fine. Postgres 16, so the ADD COLUMN with a constant default is metadata-only and would take milliseconds once it has the lock.
levels.debrief: A one-line migration waited for its lock behind a long report, and Postgres queued every other query behind the waiting migration. Nothing was busy; everything was waiting.

actions.label: Restart the pods
actions.say: Fresh pods are fast for about twenty seconds, until the first few previews hit slow favicon hosts. Then they freeze again.

actions.label: Scale from 6 to 18 pods
actions.say: Each pod still freezes, but there are three times as many, so latency drops to "bad" instead of "broken". It's spending money on a bug.

actions.label: Run uvicorn with 4 workers per pod
actions.say: Four event loops per pod instead of one: things improve a little, and each loop still freezes the same way.

actions.label: Roll back to the previous release
actions.say: Favicons are gone, and so is the problem: p99 back to 400 ms within a minute.

actions.label: Turn off the favicon feature flag
actions.say: The flag stops the favicon fetch. Latency recovers immediately, and the rest of the release stays out.

actions.label: Lower the favicon timeout to 1 s
actions.say: Each blocking call is shorter, so the freezes are shorter. Still every request on the pod waits for each favicon fetch, one at a time.

diagnosis.prompt: Why is every endpoint slow, even /healthz?
choices: The new feature is CPU-heavy, and the GIL stops the other requests from running
The favicon hosts are rate-limiting us, so the requests queue at the load balancer
fetch_favicon calls requests.get, a blocking call, inside async code: while it waits on the network the single event loop can run nothing else
The pods are out of file descriptors because of the new outbound connections
diagnosis.explain: py-spy shows the main thread (the event loop) sitting in a socket read inside requests.get. An async def that calls a synchronous library still blocks the loop, so every other request, including the health check, waits behind it.

fix.prompt: What is the right fix for the feature?
choices: Use an async HTTP client (httpx.AsyncClient) with a short timeout, or run the blocking call with await asyncio.to_thread(...)
Add more uvicorn workers so a frozen loop matters less
Cache favicons forever so the call happens less often
Switch the service to threads instead of asyncio
fix.explain: Await something that actually yields: an async client, or offload blocking work to a thread pool. More workers only hides it until traffic grows.

hints: Low CPU, high latency, every route at once: what can one call do to a whole asyncio process?
Look at what the main thread is doing right now.
levels.truth: The previews service is a single-process uvicorn asyncio app per pod (6 pods). Release 3e7d1aa added fetch_favicon, an async def that calls requests.get(timeout=8), a blocking call. Many favicon hosts are slow, so each call blocks the event loop for seconds; every request on that pod, including /healthz, waits. CPU is ~4%, memory flat, file descriptors fine. A feature flag previews.favicons exists and is on.
levels.debrief: One synchronous HTTP call inside async code held the event loop, so the whole service waited on slow favicon hosts. Low CPU with every route slow is the signature.

actions.label: systemctl restart webhooks
actions.say: Fresh process, 40 descriptors. Deliveries recover. The count starts climbing again at about 20 a minute.

actions.label: Raise LimitNOFILE to 65536 and restart
actions.say: Plenty of room now: at this rate it takes two days to fill. It will, though.

actions.label: Deploy the fix: one shared Session, created at start-up
actions.say: One pooled session reuses a handful of connections. The descriptor count sits flat at about 210.

actions.label: kill -9 2210
actions.say: The process dies mid-delivery: in-flight webhooks are lost and systemd restarts it. Same as a restart, minus the clean shutdown.

choices: The service handles more partners than 1024 descriptors allow: the limit is too low for the load
A partner's endpoint is slow, so connections pile up waiting
The disk is full, so new files cannot be opened
Each delivery creates a new requests.Session and never closes it, so sockets leak (CLOSE-WAIT) until the 1024 limit is hit
diagnosis.explain: The count climbs steadily and never falls, and almost all of it is sockets in CLOSE-WAIT: the far end closed, we never did. A high but flat count would mean the limit is too low; a climbing one is a leak.

choices: Raise the limit to 1,000,000 so it never matters
Share one Session (a connection pool) across deliveries, or close each one with a context manager; alert on descriptor count against the limit
Restart the service every 30 minutes with a timer
Lower the delivery timeout so connections close sooner
fix.explain: Fix the leak, then watch it: the descriptor count as a share of the limit is a cheap, early alert.

hints: Is the descriptor count high and flat, or climbing?
What state are those sockets in?
levels.truth: The webhooks service (pid 2210, Python) creates a new requests.Session for every delivery and never closes it, leaking a socket per delivery that ends in CLOSE-WAIT. It leaks about 20 descriptors a minute; the limit is 1024, so it fails roughly 45 minutes after each restart. Load is normal. Disk is fine.
levels.debrief: Every delivery opened a new session and never closed it, so sockets piled up in CLOSE-WAIT until the process hit its 1024-descriptor limit. Restarting hid it for forty minutes at a time.

actions.label: Raise maximumPoolSize to 256
actions.say: Nothing changes. With an unbounded queue the offer never fails, so the pool never grows past its core size of 8.

actions.label: Raise corePoolSize to 64 (hot config reload)
actions.say: Eight threads become 64. Each waits about 1.9 s on the provider, so 64 threads handle about 33 checks a second; the queue drains in a few minutes.

actions.label: Restart the service
actions.say: The queued payouts were in memory: 6,214 of them are gone and have to be replayed from the ledger. The new process fills its queue again within minutes.

actions.label: Lower the fraud-check timeout to 500 ms
actions.say: Calls fail faster, so the queue drains, but most fraud checks now time out and payouts are held for manual review.

actions.label: Bound the queue at 500 with CallerRunsPolicy
actions.say: Back-pressure: submitters slow down instead of piling work into memory. The backlog stops growing, but it is still 8 threads against 42 a second.

diagnosis.prompt: Why is latency 14 s when the provider only takes 2?
choices: The provider is rate-limiting us, so most calls wait for a token

With 8 threads each blocked about 2 s on the slow provider, the pool does 4 checks a second against 42 arriving; the rest wait in an unbounded queue, and the pool never grows because the queue never fills
Garbage collection pauses are holding up all the threads
The 3 s timeout is not being applied, so calls hang forever
diagnosis.explain: ThreadPoolExecutor queues first and grows second. An unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue never rejects an offer, so maximumPoolSize is dead config: you stay at core size and the queue absorbs the overload as latency.

fix.prompt: What should the pool look like?
choices: Keep the unbounded queue and raise maximumPoolSize further
Use Executors.newCachedThreadPool() so threads are unlimited
Size core threads for the blocking calls (threads ≈ arrival rate × wait time), bound the queue with a deliberate rejection policy, and put a circuit breaker on the provider
Move fraud checks onto the common ForkJoinPool
fix.explain: Little's law sizes it: 42/s × 2 s needs about 84 threads in flight (or virtual threads). A bounded queue makes overload visible, and a breaker stops a slow provider from taking you down with it.

hints: How many threads are actually running, and why not more?
When does a ThreadPoolExecutor add threads beyond its core size?
levels.truth: payouts-api uses a ThreadPoolExecutor(core 8, max 64, unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, AbortPolicy) for fraud checks. The fraud provider's latency rose from 120ms to ~1.9s (still under the 3s timeout). 8 threads × (1/1.9s) ≈ 4 checks/s against 42/s submitted, so 6,000+ tasks queue in memory and latency grows. Because the queue is unbounded, the pool never grows past 8. CPU is idle; GC is normal.
levels.debrief: A slow provider plus a pool that queues first and grows second: eight threads did all the work while thousands of payouts waited in an unbounded queue, and maximumPoolSize never came into play.

actions.say: It works after a messy redeploy, and your payout workers are now directly on the internet. Priya winces.

actions.say: The route is back. The next call to the bank succeeds; the retry queue drains in two minutes.

actions.label: Revert the Terraform commit and apply it through CI
actions.say: CI shows the plan: one route to add. Applied. Calls to the bank recover, and the change is on the record.

diagnosis.prompt: Why can the workers reach the ledger but not the bank?
choices: The Terraform cleanup deleted the private subnet's default route to the NAT gateway, so traffic for the internet has nowhere to go while traffic inside the VPC still works
The NAT gateway has failed and needs replacing
The workers' security group blocks outbound traffic to the internet
The bank has blocked our IP address
diagnosis.explain: Only the local 10.20.0.0/16 route is left. Inside the VPC still works; anything else is dropped. The NAT gateway itself is healthy and the security group allows all egress.

fix.prompt: What process change stops this one?
choices: Ban deleting resources from Terraform
Give the workers public IPs so they never depend on NAT
Run terraform apply only at night
Plan in the pull request so reviewers see "destroy: aws_route.private_a_default", apply only from CI, and alert on egress failures from private subnets
fix.explain: The plan would have shown a route being destroyed. Applying from laptops with -auto-approve skips the one moment where someone would have noticed.

hints: What still works, and what doesn't? What do those two have in common?
Follow the packet: instance, subnet route table, then?
levels.truth: Terraform commit 5b1e7f2 (applied from a laptop with -auto-approve) removed aws_route.private_a_default (0.0.0.0/0 → nat-0a41f) from the private subnet route table. The NAT gateway is still available in the public subnet. Security group egress allows everything. Internal VPC traffic (10.20.0.0/16) works; anything to the internet times out. The bank is healthy and has not blocked anyone.
levels.debrief: A cleanup removed the private subnet's default route to the NAT gateway. Traffic inside the VPC kept working, so it looked like the bank was down, but nothing could leave.

levels.kicker: The deploy that kept undoing itself, and doing itself again.

opening.text: The home box keeps flapping. Down for a minute and a half, up for half a minute, down again. Like clockwork.

actions.label: Stop the deploy timer
actions.say: The flapping stops: :previous stays up. Nothing deploys now, including the fix whenever it lands.

actions.label: Add TUTOR_NOTES_MODEL to the stack's env file
actions.say: The next poll builds 9c4e1ab again, and this time it starts and passes its health check. Stable on the new commit.

actions.label: git revert 9c4e1ab and push
actions.say: The next poll sees a new commit, builds it, it's healthy. Stable. The config change will need to come back properly.

actions.label: docker restart leetcode-senpai
actions.say: It restarts :previous, which was already fine. Two minutes later the timer tries 9c4e1ab again.

actions.label: Force-start 9c4e1ab and skip the health check
actions.say: The container crash-loops on the missing variable, and with the health check skipped nothing rolls it back. Down until you undo it.

diagnosis.prompt: Why does the site go down every two minutes?
choices: The box is running out of memory and the container is OOM-killed
The health check is too strict and fails healthy containers
Commit 9c4e1ab crashes on start (a missing environment variable), so each poll deploys it, it fails the health check and rolls back, and the next poll sees the same "new" commit and tries again
Docker's restart policy keeps restarting a crashed container
diagnosis.explain: The rollback works, but the deploy only records a commit once it succeeds, so main still looks new two minutes later. Automatic recovery that repeats the failure is a retry storm.

fix.prompt: What should the deploy script do differently?
choices: Poll less often, every 30 minutes
Remember a commit that failed its health check and don't retry it until main moves on, and alert when that happens
Remove the health check so deploys always go through
Retry failed commits with exponential backoff
fix.explain: One failure, one rollback, one alert. Backoff still retries the same broken image; remembering it stops the storm.

hints: What happens on every poll? What does the poll think it's looking at?
levels.truth: The home box polls GitHub every 2 minutes. Commit 9c4e1ab reads TUTOR_NOTES_MODEL from the environment, which is not set on the box, so the container crashes on start. Each poll builds it, waits 90s for health, fails, and rolls back to :previous. The deploy only records successful commits, so the next poll retries the same commit. Memory and disk are fine.
levels.debrief: A commit that crashed on start was deployed, rolled back, and deployed again every two minutes, because the deploy never remembered that it had failed.

actions.label: Restart the pods
actions.say: A new PID namespace: zero zombies, jobs work again. They start piling up at about 500 an hour.

actions.label: Raise the pod's pids limit to 32768
actions.say: Room for eight times as many zombies. It buys most of a day.

actions.label: Add tini as PID 1 (ENTRYPOINT ["tini", "--"]) and roll out
actions.say: tini reaps every orphan that lands on it. The zombie count stays at zero, and SIGTERM now reaches the worker too.

actions.label: kill -9 every <defunct> process
actions.say: Nothing happens: zombies are already dead. Only their parent calling wait() removes them, and their parent is PID 1.

diagnosis.prompt: Why can't the container start new processes?
choices: ffmpeg is leaking memory, so the container cannot allocate more
The node has run out of PIDs because other pods are busy
Each ffmpeg is still running in the background and they never finish
Each job's shell exits at once, orphaning ffmpeg onto PID 1 (the Python worker), which never wait()s for children it didn't start, so finished ffmpegs stay zombies until the pids limit is full
diagnosis.explain: The Z state means exited but not reaped, and their parent is PID 1. A normal app as PID 1 doesn't reap orphans; an init does. 4,093 zombies against a pids.max of 4,096 is the whole story.

choices: Run a real init as PID 1 (tini, or docker run --init), and have the worker wait for its own subprocesses instead of backgrounding them through a shell
Restart the workers every hour with a CronJob
Raise pids.max as high as the node allows
Run ffmpeg in a separate pod
fix.explain: An init reaps orphans and forwards signals. And code that starts a child should wait() for it: subprocess.run, or keep the Popen and call wait.

hints: What does STAT Z mean, and who is their parent?
What is PID 1 in this container, and what is PID 1 expected to do?
levels.truth: The thumbs worker runs as PID 1 (exec-form CMD, Python). For each job it runs sh -c "ffmpeg ... &": the shell exits immediately, orphaning ffmpeg, which is re-parented to PID 1. When ffmpeg finishes it becomes a zombie because the Python worker never waits for children it did not start. Zombies accumulate (~500/hour) until the cgroup pids.max (4096) is reached; then fork fails. Memory and CPU are normal.
levels.debrief: Every job orphaned an ffmpeg onto PID 1, the worker, which never reaped them. Thousands of zombies later the container hit its process limit and could not fork.
